title: Epic: M4 the agent surface, the doctor and the first tag
description:
## Background

M4 is the fourth milestone of omaddons, as the vision bead `omad-vision-8qa` defines it (its §7 M4, amended by every comment added after body revision 2). It was planned on 2026-10-24 against `main` at `c0ab5e9`: a clean tree with 2,336 `#[test]` functions across `src/` and `tests/`, no open beads, and three deferred ones (`omad-wez`, `omad-claude-mod-explore-0va5` and `omad-7ccp`). The plan was reviewed in two rounds before the owner saw it (Considerations, "How the plan was reviewed, and what filing added"), approved by the owner, and filed as these beads the same day.

These beads replace the plan document. Every bead is self-contained: an agent that has never seen the plan, the vision bead or omaddons can work any bead from its own text, the code, and the beads it names. Every decision is taken, every open question has a recorded default, and every leaf names what blocks it and what it unblocks. Where M4 departs from the vision, the decision says so and why, and H5 (`omad-m4-agent-surface-doctor-c6cm.8.5`, the vision comments) records the departure on the vision bead. Filing added one area the plan did not have, area T (test infrastructure and end-to-end scenario suites, four leaves), and split most leaves into subtasks. It changed no decision, edge, size, error code, constant or wire name of the plan.

### Where omaddons stands

**M1 made omaddons correct, M2 made it useful from a terminal, and M3 made it visible and safe for the data players actually lose.** omaddons finds every WoW client on the machine with no configuration. It verifies every archive against the client's own TOC load rules before writing anything, and runs every change through a journaled, crash-safe, undoable transaction engine. `update` keeps every client current in one undoable run. `adopt` brings hand-installed addons under management, and `sync` makes them declarative. `errors` names the addon behind a Lua error. `backup` keeps every client's `WTF/`, and a bar widget does all of it from the Omarchy desktop. Every command can answer with one JSON envelope whose errors carry runnable fixes. Two broad review passes after M3 fixed about 155 defects, and the tracker held no open work when M4 was planned.

**What M1–M3 leave unfinished is the part the vision calls the product's promise to agents** (vision goal G4: "the first command an agent guesses works"; "discovery via `capabilities`, `doctor` and `robot-docs`"; "plans are stored: a dry run can be applied exactly"), plus the part it calls the promise to everyone (vision goal G7: "`doctor` follows the world-class doctor contract"):

- **An agent cannot learn omaddons from omaddons.** There is no `capabilities`, no `robot-docs`, no schema for any command's `data`, and no installed skill. Today an agent learns the tool by reading a 2,804-line README or by trial and error. The README's own "For coding agents" block is hand-written and can drift.
- **The contract is not frozen, and nothing would notice if it drifted.** No golden file records the wire names, their types, which are always present, or the CLI's flags and defaults. `error.details` is an untyped value with no declared keys, and several registries (recommendation actions, env vars, NDJSON events, failure-mode ids) are scattered literals.
- **A preview binds only for destructive commands.** `--dry-run` of `install`, `update`, `sync` or `copy` shows a plan, but the real run re-plans from scratch: a release that lands in between, another client's change, or a hand edit in a folder it replaces can make the real run differ from what an agent showed its user. Even M3's bindings compare only record generations under the commit lock, which no editor or sync tool ever moves. `plan_id`, `apply` and `plan_not_found` are reserved and unused.
- **There is no doctor.** When something goes wrong that recovery cannot settle (a journal a newer build wrote, a journal holding a line this build cannot read, a restore whose recovery met a state it does not recognize), README says "manual repair" and points at a milestone that does not exist yet. Records that two clients doubled before the shared-AddOns rule, credentials readable by other users, a stale widget, orphaned stages and corrupted cache blobs are each reported somewhere, or nowhere. None of them can be repaired, reversibly and with consent, by one command.
- **Typos are handled, misplaced words are not.** `omaddons retail update`, the first guess of many agents, gets `omaddons help`. `-t all` is not a selector. No usage-fix test checks that a suggested fix actually runs.
- **No shell completions.**

### What M4 delivers

M4 makes omaddons **self-describing, previewable end to end, self-repairing, and frozen**:

1. **`omaddons capabilities --json`.** Every command, flag, alias, exit code, error and warning code (with retryability and the typed shape of its `details`), recommendation action, failure mode, environment variable, limit, source, family, client-rules row and `-t` form. One call, offline, in a few milliseconds, generated from the live clap tree and the code's registries.
2. **`omaddons robot-docs`.**
   - `guide` is the agent handbook: the core loop, how to read an envelope, the safety model, a "will never do" list, and eight recipes, one per canonical intent, each run as an end-to-end test.
   - `schema [<command>]` is the JSON Schema of every command's `data`, of the envelope and of the stderr events. The contract suite validates every live envelope it produces against these schemas.
   - `errors` is the full code catalog with fixes.
   - `install-skill` writes the guide as `SKILL.md` where Claude Code (and, on request, other agents) looks for skills. `skills/omaddons/SKILL.md` in the repository is the same bytes, held so by a test. The guide's identity is a content digest stamped after its frontmatter, so the doctor repairs an installed skill whose guide changed, never one that merely came from another build.
3. **Intent inference, finished.** `omaddons retail update` suggests `omaddons update -t retail`. `omaddons status retail`, `omaddons info dbm retail` and `omaddons remove dbm retail` say that `retail` is a client, and the last changes nothing until the user corrects it. `-t all` selects every client where a command accepts several. A mistyped client id gets the closest one. A corpus of wrong invocations checks that each suggested fix not only parses but runs, and that each wrong invocation changed nothing.
4. **Previews that bind everywhere, and stored plans.**
   - Every command that changes addons (`install`, `update`, `pin`, `unpin`, `adopt`, `sync`, `copy`) now returns a precondition token from `--dry-run` and honours `--if-match`, like `remove`, `undo`, `backup restore`, `backup prune` and `errors dismiss` since M3. The token carries an approval witness of every file the plan would replace or remove, edited or clean, and the commit checks it again under its lock, so a hand edit after the preview is caught, not committed over.
   - Each such dry run also stores its typed intent for 24 hours. `omaddons apply <plan_id>` commits, on each target, exactly that plan or nothing, holds the plan's lease so two applications never split it, and reports every target's outcome. A release that landed since the preview, a change on any affected client, a binary upgrade, a missing input or an expired plan each give `plan_stale` with what changed. `omaddons plans show <plan_id>` tells an agent that lost the output whether it committed.
   - The bar widget's Update buttons now preview, and run the plan directly only when it matches the row and needs no further approval; a new dependency, replaced local edits or another source opens the dialog.
5. **`omaddons doctor`, to the world-class doctor contract.**
   - Bare `doctor` is read-only. It checks 46 failure modes (44 detectors, plus two the runtime raises itself: a detector that crashed, and one cut short) over omaddons' own state, the clients' managed folders, caches, the widget, the skill and credentials, and reports each finding with evidence and an exact remediation. A check cut short by its budget is reported as incomplete, never as healthy.
   - `doctor fix` repairs the auto-fixable ones with consent. A fix run is one engine transaction of kind `repair`, made of primitive steps each journaled ahead: backed up verbatim, recorded in history, and undone by `omaddons undo <tx>` or `omaddons doctor undo <run>` while nothing it touched has changed since. It never deletes: what it removes it moves into a quarantine, and only `doctor gc` deletes, never what an unfinished transaction still needs.
   - The rest of the surface: `explain`, `health`, `ls`, `diff`, `gc`, `capabilities`, `robot-docs` and `--robot-triage`.
   - The stuck states that README calls "manual repair" today become findings with repairs gated behind `--force --yes`. The repair suspends the stuck journal; nothing is lost, and undo puts it back only while doing so cannot replay stale instructions over newer work. A stuck repair of its own blocks only the files it protects, and one whose journal this build cannot read fails closed until it is set aside.
   - `status` reads the same detector registry (its fast tiers), so `status` and `doctor` can never disagree about what is wrong.
   - A five-property safety harness (reversibility, idempotence, crash recovery, concurrency, detector repeatability) plus a fixture per fixer runs in every gate.
6. **Shell completions** (`omaddons completions bash|zsh|fish|elvish|powershell`).
7. **Durability decided.** The audit log the doctor contract requires (`actions.jsonl`) is group-committed once per transaction, derived cache files stop being fsynced, and directory fsyncs are deferred, through handles that survive renames, to explicit barriers that report their errors before success. On btrfs an install's lock window drops from 62 fsyncs to the count G3 (`omad-7ccp`, group commit, derived writes and deferred directory fsyncs) derives from the boundaries it counts first; the forecast is at most 44, about 60 ms of its 165 ms (the measurement and estimate recorded on G3's own bead, which is the formerly deferred durability bead, reused). The deferred directory fsyncs' further cut is measured and reported, not promised.
8. **The freeze.** The contract's naming rules hold from the first slice, and a pre-freeze audit finishes making it consistent while that is still free. Then a semantic manifest pins every output's types, requiredness and nullability and every input's flags, defaults and grammar, with a readable names list beside it, and the first tag, `v0.1.0`, records it as the released baseline. From the tag on, the gate compares every change with that baseline and refuses one without the version bump it needs, however the current golden was regenerated.

None of this weakens an M1–M3 guarantee. Every new write goes through fsx; every repair is a journaled transaction; every new error carries an executable fix; dry runs still leave `<state>` untouched; and the envelope keeps `schema_version` "1.0" until the tag.

### Why this is the right M4

- **The vision assigns exactly this scope to M4** (vision §7 M4), and three earlier milestones handed work to it explicitly: stored plans (M3-D9, "M4's `plan_id` can embed the same `Precondition`"), the doctor's manual-repair automation (README "`journal_pending` that does not clear"), the doubled shared records (README Known limitations), the `internal` errors' fix (DEC-5), and the durability decision (G3, deferred "until M4 is planned").
- **Freezing is only cheap now.** One owner and a widget built in the same repository are the only consumers today, so every inconsistency the pre-freeze audit finds costs one commit. After the tag, the same fix costs a major contract version.
- **Agents are the main users of a CLI whose product is its contract.** The canonical intents (vision §5.10) become two commands at most, each tested end to end. An agent that has never seen omaddons can be pointed at it and work correctly.
- **The doctor turns the engine's honesty into recoverability.** M3 made every persisted format fail closed, which is right. But "left for manual repair" is a dead end for a user without the source code. The doctor gives each such state a name, evidence, a consented and reversible repair, and a test that proves the repair round-trips.

### How to read the M4 beads

#### Who reads what

- **The owner** approved the plan before it was filed. That approval is the only owner step in M4 (Considerations, "Owner involvement"); no bead waits on a person. This body, the decision table and the success criteria are written for the owner too.
- **The filing agent** turned the plan into these beads. Its record is the last of the plan's comments on this epic (comment 20 in the table below).
- **The agents that implement M4** read their bead. It carries everything it needs: the background and every decision it obeys (restated, with the reason and the rejected alternative where that matters), the technical approach, the acceptance criteria, a test plan that names its logging, the considerations, the dependencies with the reason for each, and the common rules. A section number such as `§6.9.1` appears only as provenance after the content it labels. The section itself is carried by one of the comments on this epic ("Where the rest of the plan lives", below).

#### Words

- A **target** is one WoW client (one flavor folder or one private-server root). **Managed** means omaddons has a record for it.
- The **contract** is everything a program can rely on in omaddons' output: the JSON envelope, each command's `data` keys, error and warning codes and the typed shape of each code's `details`, recommendation actions, failure-mode ids, NDJSON event names and fields, exit codes, flags with their defaults and value grammars, and the keys of the files omaddons persists. Member order inside a JSON object is not part of it. **Freezing** the contract (at the first tag) means that from then on a change to any of these follows the version rules, checked against the released baseline: an additive change (emitting more, accepting more) needs the same major and a higher minor `schema_version`; a breaking change (emitting less or less predictably, accepting less, changing a default) or an unclassified one needs a higher major; a persisted format's change needs its own kind's version bump instead (M4-D56).
- A **wire name** is one entry of the contract written as a line of text (for example `output install data.items[].status string!`). The **golden** is the committed **semantic manifest** of the contract, `tests/contract/manifest.json` (every output's types, requiredness and nullability, every input's flags, defaults and grammar), with its readable projection of wire names, `tests/contract/wire_names.txt`. The **released baseline** is the manifest of the last released contract, `tests/contract/released/<version>.json`, which only the release procedure advances.
- **Capabilities** is `omaddons capabilities --json`: the machine-readable description of the whole CLI, generated from the code. **Doctor capabilities** is `omaddons doctor capabilities --json`: the same for the doctor.
- The **guide** is `omaddons robot-docs guide`: the Markdown handbook for agents. The **skill** is the same bytes installed where coding agents look for skills (`SKILL.md`).
- A **precondition token** (M3-D46) is a `pc1:` string that describes exactly what a previewed command will do. For the engine-backed commands it includes an **approval witness** of everything the plan reads, replaces or removes (M4-D60); M3's five tokens (`remove`, `undo`, `backup restore`, `backup prune`, `errors dismiss`) are unchanged. `--if-match <token>` makes the real run do that or nothing (`plan_stale`), on each target.
- A **stored plan** is a precondition token plus the **typed intent** it binds (the command's normalized arguments, never an argv to re-parse), kept for 24 hours under a **plan id**. `omaddons apply <plan_id>` executes it; `omaddons plans show <plan_id>` inspects it.
- A **finding** is one instance of a **failure mode** (an `fm-<subsystem>-<slug>` id), found by a **detector**, with a stable, resource-specific **instance key**. A **fixer** repairs it. A **repair** is one doctor fix run: one engine transaction of kind `repair`, made of **primitive** steps (one filesystem operation each), plus its **run directory** `<run>`.
- A **resource set** is the canonical read and write paths (and named resources) an operation touches; two overlap when one path is the other or its ancestor (M4-D62). A stuck repair journal **fences** its resources: overlapping writes are refused, everything else proceeds.
- A **slice** is a set of leaves with a demonstrable exit (Success Criteria, "Slice demos"). Slices are the milestone's progress measure.
- A **design gate** (added at filing, from common rule 14): a leaf that adds or changes a journal shape, a recovery rule, a binding rule, a deletion rule or a durability rule closes only when its own adversarial matrix passes. The ten design-gate leaves are listed under Considerations.

#### How a leaf with subtasks is worked

- **The leaf is the unit of closure.** Its acceptance criteria are what must be true before any bead it blocks may start. Subtasks split the work, not the closure: each subtask is one coherent piece of work that lands as one commit passing `argc gate` on its own and leaves `main` consistent. A size-L leaf stays one bead for this reason: no dependent ever sees half of it.
- **Wiring.** Each subtask is a `parent-child` child of its leaf, and its order among its siblings is given by `blocks` edges between them, kept as shallow as the code allows (two subtasks that touch different files and do not need each other's code are not chained). Every leaf is a child of its area epic, and every area epic of this epic. Epics carry no `blocks` edges: an epic with an open blocker would make `br` hide every child as parent-blocked.
- **The leaf's blockers gate every subtask.** While a leaf has an open blocker, `br` reports its subtasks as blocked through their parent, so no part of a leaf starts before the leaf may. While a leaf has open subtasks, the leaf itself is held by them and does not appear in `br ready`.
- **Claim a subtask, not the leaf.** `br ready --parent <leaf id>` lists the ready ones. Each subtask's body starts with "Part k of N of KEY (`<id>`, <leaf title>). If this is the last open subtask of that bead, verify its acceptance criteria and close it as its body says." The agent that closes the last open subtask then verifies every acceptance criterion of the leaf (they are the leaf's, not any one subtask's) and closes the leaf with `br close <leaf id> --reason "done: <evidence> · found: <ids>"`. Until the leaf is closed, every bead it blocks stays blocked.
- **How leaves were split.**
  - A size-S leaf usually has no subtasks; the leaf is the work. A size-S `feature` gets one companion test subtask (`Tests: …`) when its integration tests are a distinct piece of work.
  - A size-M leaf has 2 to 5 subtasks; a size-L leaf 3 to 7.
  - Every `feature` leaf, and every M or L leaf that ships behaviour, has at least one test subtask (`Tests:` or `E2E:`) for its integration and end-to-end suites, ordered after the subtasks it tests.
  - A design-gate leaf has a subtask for its adversarial matrix (failpoints, journaled steps, repeated recovery, injected I/O failures) unless an implementation subtask already contains it. Its design gate is passed only when that subtask is closed.
  - DEC-1, no stubs: all of a command's registry touch points (its clap variant, its `COMMANDS` row with every M4 field, `command_name` and dispatch, the help layout, contract matrix rows, the `special.rs` row, `cli_skeleton` literals, its `CLI_PATHS` row, its README section) land in one subtask, the one that adds the command.
  - Unit tests ship with the code they test, in the same subtask and commit. The test subtask is for integration and end-to-end suites, crash and concurrency matrices, and cross-cutting property tests.
  - A subtask never adds a wire shape its leaf does not own.

#### The test and logging standard

The owner asked that M4's beads include comprehensive unit tests and end-to-end test scripts with detailed logging, so that after implementation every behaviour can be shown to work and every failure can be diagnosed from its log alone. Area T exists for that.

- **What "end-to-end test script" means here.** A Rust integration test that drives the real `omaddons` binary through a scenario on a synthetic home (`tests/*.rs`, `assert_cmd`, `TestEnv`). M4-D47 rejected shell fixture scripts ("a second test language, and shell scripts that must clean up after themselves"), and the house rules ban `rm -rf` even in test scripts. The one runner script M4 adds is an `argc` task.
- **T1 (`omad-m4-agent-surface-doctor-c6cm.9.1`) adds `tests/common/tlog.rs`,** a structured step log. Its API:
  - `let log = tlog!();` (or `TestLog::new(suite, test)`) creates `<CARGO_TARGET_TMPDIR>/test-logs/<suite>/<test>/` with `steps.jsonl` (one JSON object per step) and `transcript.md` (the same, readable). A rerun replaces the directory.
  - `log.step("label")` opens a phase; `log.note(text)`; `log.json(label, &value)`.
  - `log.run(&env, &argv) -> Ran` runs the real binary through `TestEnv::command()` and records the argv, the test's environment overrides (any variable whose name contains `TOKEN`, `SECRET` or `CREDENTIAL` redacted), the working directory, the start time and `elapsed_ms`, the exit code, stdout (the envelope, parsed), stderr (NDJSON events, parsed), the `net.log` lines this run added and the failpoints armed. `Ran::{ok(), exit(n), envelope(), data(), error_code(), warnings(), commands()}`; a failing `Ran` assertion names the step, the expected and actual exit, the error code and message, and the transcript path.
  - `log.tree(label, root)` and `log.assert_unchanged(label, root)` record and compare tree hashes (modes and symlink targets included), logging the first differing paths.
  - On panic, a guard prints `test log: <path>` and the last 20 steps. `OMADDONS_TEST_LOG=verbose` echoes every step live (run with `--nocapture`). `OMADDONS_TEST_LOG` is a harness variable, registered in the env-var registry with kind `harness`.
  - Captures are bounded (1 MiB per stream per step, 64 MiB per test), and a truncation is logged, never silent. The logs hold only synthetic `TestEnv` homes and never read the developer's real `HOME`. They live under `CARGO_TARGET_TMPDIR`, so `cargo clean` removes them and nothing is committed.
- **Who uses it.** Every M4 integration or end-to-end test that runs more than one command uses `TestLog`: each phase of a scenario is a `step`, and every state assertion goes through `log.tree`/`assert_unchanged` or logs the values it compares. Every bead that writes such a test is blocked by T1 (an edge added at filing), so T1 is claimed first (Considerations, "The graph with area T").
- **Unit tests** in `src/` do not use `TestLog`. They are table-driven, with a name per case and assertion messages that name the case and show the input and the output.
- **Every test plan in a bead** has a `Logging` part: the steps each scenario records, the trees it hashes, and what a failure prints.
- **The runner.** `argc e2e [FILTER]` runs the M4 end-to-end suites with `OMADDONS_TEST_LOG=verbose` and prints the log root at the end. It is a convenience: the gate's `cargo test` runs the same tests.
- **The slice demos are tests.** T2, T3 and T4 turn the exit demos of slices 1–3 into suites that run in every gate after the slice lands (Success Criteria, "Slice demos").

## Goals

- **G-M4-1 Self-describing.** An agent with no prior knowledge learns everything it needs from the binary itself, in at most three calls: `omaddons capabilities --json`, `omaddons robot-docs guide`, `omaddons status --json`. Every fact in those outputs is generated from the code, so it cannot drift from what the code does. Every command's output has a published JSON Schema, and the contract suite validates real output against it.
- **G-M4-2 The first guess works.** A plausible wrong invocation yields a usage error whose fix is the command the user meant. That covers a misplaced client name, a typo of a command, flag, value or client id, `-t all`, and `apply` vs `adopt --apply`. Each such fix is proven to run, not only to parse. A fix never turns the user's verb into a different command that changes something.
- **G-M4-3 What was previewed is what runs, target by target.**
  - Every command that changes addons can be previewed with `--dry-run` and then run bound to that preview, by token (`--if-match`) or by stored plan (`apply <plan_id>`).
  - **The guarantee is per target.** On each target the bound run commits exactly the operations the preview approved, or none of them. A run over several targets commits one transaction per target, as it always has (M1, vision comment 269), so it can end partial after a late conflict or an I/O failure. It then reports each target as committed, unchanged, stale or failed, with its transaction id, and never calls the whole run atomic (M4-D61).
  - **The approval covers what the preview saw, not only the record generations** (M4-D60): every file of every folder the plan replaces or removes, clean or edited; every name it creates; its local inputs; a copy's source folders; the rules that judged it. The commit checks all of it again under the lock, and the operations it re-judges there must equal the approved ones.
  - **What the guarantee is against.** Other omaddons processes are serialized by the global lock and by one applier per plan (M4-D61). Other writers (an editor, a file-sync tool) are caught by those checks up to the moment before the first change, and each move then re-checks only the identity of what it moves. omaddons promises no compare-and-swap against arbitrary writers, because the filesystem offers none.
  - "Anything else" is named precisely: a new release, a change on an affected client, another binary, an expired plan, a missing input, a plan already applied.
  - **An approval can be inspected and reconciled.** `omaddons plans show <plan_id>` says, offline and without writing, what was approved and what history records of it, so an agent that lost an `apply`'s output learns whether it committed before it does anything else (M4-D63).
  - The bar widget's Update buttons apply a plan directly only when its selection matches the row the user pressed and it needs no further approval (new dependencies, removals, replaced local edits, a different source). Anything else opens the dialog (M4-D28).
- **G-M4-4 Diagnosable and repairable.**
  - `omaddons doctor` names every broken state omaddons can detect in what it owns or manages. Each finding carries concrete evidence and an exact remediation. A check that ran out of budget or entries says so: incomplete coverage is never reported as healthy.
  - Every auto-fixable state is repaired by one consented command that backs up verbatim, never deletes, and is proven by a fixture that round-trips. A repair can be undone byte for byte as long as no later change overlaps what it touched; once one does, undo refuses before moving anything, and the kept bytes stay inspectable.
  - The states README calls "manual repair" today each get a name, an explanation and a guarded repair.
  - `status` and `doctor` never disagree about what is wrong.
- **G-M4-5 Frozen and enforced.** At the first tag the contract is consistent (audited), complete (a semantic manifest of every input the CLI accepts and every output it emits, with a readable names list beside it) and enforced: every later change is compared with the released baseline, and one that does not carry its version bump fails the gate, however the current golden was regenerated. Every exit site maps to a published code in the right dictionary. Repeated runs print identical bytes.
- **G-M4-6 No new risk to the engine's guarantees.**
  - Every new write goes through fsx, and every repair is a journaled transaction that recovers like any other.
  - Dry runs still leave `<state>` untouched, and the global lock is still held only for commit windows.
  - The doctor never writes `WTF/`.
  - A build from before M4 never destroys what M4 wrote: the M3 build is characterized against M4 state, and README states the result.

## Success Criteria

The M4 checkpoint. H6 (`omad-m4-agent-surface-doctor-c6cm.8.6`, the M4 checkpoint and the first tag) runs each criterion and records the evidence in its close reason in the M2/M3 format `[x] N <criterion>: <evidence>`, with the commit hash, test names, timings and every `SKIP` line quoted. These criteria amend vision §7 "M4 checkpoints"; each amendment is marked below and explained in the decision log. The slice demos are recorded on this epic as each slice lands ("Slice demos", at the end of this section). This section is what is true when every child of this epic is closed.

**Pre-accepted `SKIP`s.** The plan's approval accepts exactly these in advance, so H6 never needs an owner decision at close:

- `keyless_installs_forever` (`tests/real_machine.rs`), which M2 and M3 already allow through `OMADDONS_ALLOW_SKIP` while the Forever client's guard (`forever_guard()`) stands;
- the bind-mount and size-limited-tmpfs sandbox tests (`unshare -rm`), where unprivileged user namespaces are unavailable;
- the `zsh -n` and `fish --no-execute` syntax checks of generated completions, where those shells are not installed (bash's check is never skipped).

Any other `SKIP` means the criterion is not met. It is recorded as unmet, with its reason, and a bug is filed `discovered-from` H6 and added as H6's blocker. H6 waits on that dependency, and is never deferred to a person. (M3 deferred its checkpoint for an owner decision in that case; M4 does not.)

**The compatibility characterizations are never skipped.** An older commit that needs an older compiler is built with the toolchain it records: both `af10e34` (M3's planning commit) and `c0ab5e9` pin `1.97.1` in `rust-toolchain.toml`, which rustup installs on demand. Otherwise a provenance-verified binary of that commit is used. If neither can be had, the no-destructive-downgrade criterion (16) is unmet and the checkpoint says so: compiler inconvenience is not evidence that storage is safe.

1. **Capabilities.**

Failure modes are summarized (`count`, `subsystems`) with a pointer to `doctor capabilities`, which lists every id, and the count equals the registry's.

2. **Schemas.** `omaddons robot-docs schema` gives a JSON Schema for every command path in `app::COMMANDS`, for the envelope and for every NDJSON event.

   - Every JSON envelope snapshot in the repository validates too: a walker test reads every `.snap` file (159 at `c0ab5e9`: 140 under `tests/`, 19 under `src/`; the contract matrix covers 105 of them), keeps each whose body parses as a JSON envelope, and validates it against its `command`'s schema.
   - Validation in tests is strict: an emitted key that the schema lacks fails it, except under the declared `OPAQUE` paths (a registry, `contract::OPAQUE`, of the few deliberately unconstrained application values, such as config values, each with its reason). The strict transform is itself tested on `$ref`, maps, tagged unions and composition: it admits no unknown field and rejects no valid variant field.

Every observed `details` object validates against its code's specification, so a `details.changed` that turned into a string fails the suite.

9. **The doctor's safety harness**, in every gate.
   - Bare `doctor` changes nothing outside `<state>/doctor/`. That is checked by tree hashes of `<state>`, `<cache>`, `<config>` and every client dir, over every fixture.
   - Every auto-fixer round-trips: corrupt → `doctor` finds it → `doctor fix` → the fixture asserts healthy → `doctor undo` → the subject tree is byte-identical to the corrupted state, modes and symlinks included. A fixer's own subjects are never excluded from that comparison: a set-aside's subject is the original journal, in-flight file, stage and both snapshot halves.
   - A second `doctor fix` takes 0 actions. It exits 0 when no finding of the fixed ids remains, or 1 when only unfixable instances remain, and never 2.
   - A crash (a real `abort`) at every repair-journal failpoint and at every primitive boundary of every fixer (each lowered write, chmod and rename) is recovered by the next lock-taking command. Afterwards the whole subject set equals the before state when the crash preceded the durable `done`, and the after state from `done` on; a mixture fails. Recovery itself is crashed at every primitive inverse and repeated three times, every preserved original is accounted for, and the harness asserts that every primitive boundary of every action kind actually fired. No boundary is sampled away to save time.
   - Two concurrent fixers serialize: one repairs, the other takes 0 actions or exits 5 `concurrency_lost`. They never interleave. Fixes whose resources overlap (a directory and its child, a rename's destination) are refused together, never run in one transaction.
   - Detectors are repeatable: two diagnoses of one state give identical findings.
   - Every write lands inside a declared write scope, and no code path renames or deletes the global lock file.
   - `set(fixers) == set(fixtures with a fixer)`, and every detector has a fixture that triggers it and a clean home that does not.
   - *(Amended: concurrency is "serialize and re-plan" per M4-D45, not "exactly one exits 5".)*

11. **Stuck states are named and repairable.** Every state where recovery stops for manual repair at `c0ab5e9` has a finding with a correct title in both `status` and `doctor`:

While nothing that overlaps the suspended set has changed, `doctor undo` reactivates it byte-identical, after which recovery behaves exactly as before the repair. After an overlapping change (a later install on that client, say), `doctor undo` refuses with `undo_conflict` before moving anything, and the set stays inspectable in quarantine.

## Non-Goals

- **CurseForge and Wago** (bring-your-own-key sources), their `secrets` and `--online` doctor checks, fingerprint adoption, and the GitHub GraphQL batch path all stay in M5 (vision §7 M5, M2-D22). M4 pulls forward only the doctor checks for credentials and sources that exist today (M4-D51).
- **Release engineering beyond the tag**, all M5: a version scheme beyond `0.1.0`, a CHANGELOG, a PKGBUILD, packaged completions, a man page (`clap_mangen`) and the binary-size target. M4 makes the first tag and nothing else of release engineering.
- **An MCP server, a daemon, a GUI or a TUI** (vision D3). M4 makes a later MCP adapter cheaper, because `capabilities` and the schemas are its contract, but builds none.
- **Executing a deserialized engine plan.** `apply` executes the stored typed intent, re-planning bound to its token (M4-D23). Serializing `TargetPlan.work` and `Inspected` is not done, and nothing in M4 needs it.
- **An invocation-wide atomic transaction across clients.** The guarantee is per target, as the engine's one-transaction-per-target design has always been (M4-D61); partial outcomes are reported, never hidden.
- **A compare-and-swap against arbitrary writers.** omaddons checks everything it approved under its lock, and each operation's identity, but no filesystem primitive lets it rename a directory only if nobody has written into it a microsecond earlier (M4-D60).
- **`plans list`.** `plans show` inspects one approval by id; listing every preview is not added (M4-D63).
- **Dynamic shell completion** of client ids and addon names. clap's dynamic completion is unstable; static completion covers commands, flags and fixed values.
- **Doctor repairs that edit user content.** The doctor never parses or edits SavedVariables, `config.toml`, `addons.toml` or `catalog.d` files. A broken config is reported with its line and column, never rewritten. The one fixer that touches an addon folder (flattening a nested unmanaged folder) is off by default (M4-D39).
- **Rewriting `history.jsonl`.** It stays append-only, and history findings are reports (M4-D49).
- **Making the doctor a CI gate or a pre-commit hook.** `doctor --quick` makes that possible; wiring it into anything is not M4's.
- **Shipping the Claude Code mod** (`omad-claude-mod-explore-0va5`). It stays deferred and owner-led. M4's `capabilities` and schemas are what such a mod would read.
- **Re-verifying Forever after its 2026-11-04 launch** (`omad-wez`). It stays a dated deferral outside M4. If it lands during M4, it runs on M4's code, and nothing in M4 depends on it.

### The graph with area T

The plan computed its graph from its own text by script, not by hand: every leaf's "Blocked by" list, every "Unblocks" list as its exact inverse, no cycle, earliest start and finish, slack and critical paths, and a lane schedule. Filing reran the same computation with area T's edges (leaf level, S = 1, M = 2, L = 3).

- **The critical path stays 25 units:** E1 → E2 → E3 → E6 → E7 → F2 → H1 → H2 → H4 → H5 → H6, the doctor and its repairs, then the freeze.
- **Area T adds two more zero-slack chains.** T4 waits for every slice-3 leaf and H4 waits for T4, so E1 → … → F2 → F9 → T4 → H4 → H5 → H6 and E1 → … → F2 → G3 → T4 → H4 → H5 → H6 are now 25 units too. ### Owner involvement

M3's real-machine and desktop steps waited for an owner go-ahead. M4 needs the owner exactly once: **approving the plan** before the beads were filed. That approval is done.

That approval is also the go-ahead for the checkpoint's real-machine and desktop runs, each listed exactly in H6's bead, each read-only or undone, and none touching the `Forever` client's state:

- the doctor on the real home (`doctor` and `doctor fix --dry-run`, read-only);
- one update previewed and applied on a non-Forever client, then undone;
- the widget's Update preview on the live bar;
- a doctor repair from the Issues view, undone;
- `install-skill --dry-run` against the real home, and a real install into a tempdir only.

**Decided, so nothing waits on a person:**

- **The real skill directory.** Nothing in M4 installs the skill into the real `$HOME/.claude/skills/`. A skill there is loaded by every Claude Code session on the machine, which is the owner's call, made with one command whenever they like. The checkpoint proves the default path resolves (the dry run) and the install works (the tempdir).
- **An unexpected `SKIP`** is a failed criterion (Success Criteria), not a question.

No bead is ever filed whose next step belongs to a person (CLAUDE.md, "Blocked on a Human"), and no step of H6 waits on one.

### Two owner-visible changes

Both are recorded in README and on the vision bead:

1. Dry runs of the addon-changing commands now write a small plan file under `<cache>/plans/` (M4-D21). It is safe to delete, like everything in `<cache>`, is swept after 24 hours, and the store has hard quotas.
2. The contract freezes at `v0.1.0`. After that, adding even one JSON key needs a minor `schema_version` bump, checked against the released baseline (M4-D56).

### Design gates

Ten leaves introduce new protocols and close only when their own adversarial matrices are green (common rule 14: every failpoint they add, every journaled step, repeated recovery, and injected I/O failure where they write):

- D1 and D2 (`of_plan` tokens and approval witnesses on engine commands, and the dry-run and no-op checks);
- D8 (the approval checked again under the commit lock);
- D5 (`apply` and its lease);
- E11 (the classifier, a simulation of recovery, held to recovery by a differential test);
- E5 (the repair journal of primitive steps, its write-ahead and its recovery);
- E14 (fences and activation barriers, and recovery's new order);
- E7 (undo of repairs, its guards and its activation-aware inverses);
- E8 (gc's retention plan, which deletes);
- G3 (group commit and deferred directory fsyncs through explicit barriers, with a written power-loss argument per ordering point).

Expect them to take longer than their size label. Each has a subtask for its matrix (or an implementation subtask that contains it), and its gate is passed only when that part is closed. A gate that changes a leaf's size or edges triggers the recomputation above. F9 integrates across fixers; it never discovers whether a leaf's own protocol works.

### Critical path and staffing

The order the edges enforce puts correctness first: approval witnesses and resource modelling, then semantic contract generation, then primitive repair and activation recovery, then fixers and gc, then the widget and reconciliation, and durability last, optimized against the settled protocols.

- Staff E3, E5, E7, E11, E14 and F2 with the engine and runtime specialists.
- Start D1 and E11 at once: each heads a chain one unit behind the critical path. Start T1 at once too (above).
- Claim critical-path leaves first whenever several are ready (`bv` ranks by it). With area T, F9 and G3 are critical-path leaves.
- Let the intent area (C) absorb slips: it has the most slack.

### The contract's rules hold from slice 1, and H1 is their final audit (M4-D55)

A1 and A3 establish the canonical naming, nullability and command-path rules before dependent surfaces are generated, and A3's rule test fails any new shape that breaks them (existing violations sit on an allowlist, `tests/contract/rules_allowlist.txt`, that may only shrink). A known pre-release inconsistency is corrected in the leaf that owns the surface, with an explicit compatibility note in its close comment and the widget and guide edited in the same commit, rather than carried through the milestone to be repaired across every consumer at the end. Otherwise leaves add wire names (DEC-4) and list them in their close comments. H1 empties the allowlist and audits what remains. The freeze is the last code change before the checkpoint.

### `SKILL.md` churn is expected and mechanical

Once B1 lands, every leaf that adds a code, an action or a command changes the guide's generated tables. The `skill_md_is_the_guide` test then fails with the exact command to regenerate the file, `OMADDONS_UPDATE_SKILL=1 cargo test --test skill`, which renders from a hermetic `TestEnv` (never the developer's real `HOME` or config) and which the leaf runs and commits. That is not a script editing code (CLAUDE.md "No Script-Based Changes"). It is the binary's own output, committed as an embedded asset, exactly as insta snapshots are accepted.

### README is the product contract

Each leaf that ships a user-visible surface updates its README section in the same commit. H4 is the final consistency pass, not the first mention.

### The decisions that shape the milestone

The full log (M4-D1 to M4-D63: decision, reason, rejected alternatives, implementing leaves) is in the four decision-log comments on this epic, with every departure from the vision collected at the end of the fourth. These are the ones that shape everything else:

| Decision | One line |
|---|---|
| M4-D2 | One contract registry (`src/contract/`) feeds `capabilities`, `robot-docs`, the wire-name golden and help. A fact clap cannot give is declared once beside the command and verified by a test, never written twice. |
| M4-D7 | The guide, `skills/omaddons/SKILL.md` and the installed skill are one artifact: hand-written prose with generated tables, rendered by the binary, byte-identical in all three places. |
| M4-D19 | Every command that changes addons gets `--if-match`. Its token is computed from the engine's own plan (`of_plan`) and covers releases, expected hashes, the folder plan and the rules that judged it. |
| M4-D60 | The token carries an approval witness of everything the plan reads, replaces or removes, checked again under the commit lock with the re-judged operations; the guarantee's scope is stated, with no promise of a compare-and-swap against arbitrary writers. |
| M4-D20 | Both races stale a preview: a concurrent change, and a release landing in between. `apply` revalidates its sources. A typed `--if-match` keeps its command's freshness. |
| M4-D21 | Stored plans live in `<cache>/plans/`, not `<state>/plans/`: plans are derived and expire in 24 h, so dry runs stay state-free (a departure from vision §5.6, recorded). |
| M4-D23 | `apply <plan_id>` executes a stored, typed, normalized intent bound to its stored token. It is neither a deserialized engine plan nor a re-parsed argv: re-planning bound to the token proves equality, and the intent cannot name a command that is not storable. |
| M4-D61 | One applier per plan (a lease), and the guarantee is per target: each target commits exactly the approved operations or none, and a multi-target run reports each target's outcome. |
| M4-D63 | `plans show` inspects an approval and reconciles it with history, offline, so a lost `apply` output is never answered by a blind retry. |
| M4-D29 | One detector registry serves `doctor`, `doctor health` and `status`. Each detector declares a tier (`cached`, `quick`, `default`, `deep`), so `status --cached` stays under 5 ms. |
| M4-D31 | A doctor fix run is one engine transaction of kind `repair`, with its own write-ahead journal family, history line and undo. The doctor's run directory is a view of that transaction (vision D26), not a second undo system. |
| M4-D35 | Quarantine stays on the victim's own filesystem: `<run>/quarantine/` for state, `<cache>/quarantine/<run id>/` for cache, `<meta>/snapshots/<tx>.repair/quarantine/` for client paths. A rename never crosses a mount. |
| M4-D38 | The stuck journal states (too new, unreadable, an unrecognized step, a marker that names another target, no readable target) get a "set aside" repair that suspends the journal set into quarantine. It is gated behind `--force --yes` and never part of a default fix; its undo reactivates the set behind an activation barrier, and only while nothing it depends on has changed. |
| M4-D62 | Fixer conflicts, stuck-repair fences, undo conflicts and gc's pins all use one canonical resource model, so overlapping work is refused and unrelated work continues. |
| M4-D45 | The concurrency property is "serialize and re-plan" (vision D24), not "exactly one exits 5": a second fixer waits for the lock, re-plans and takes no action for what the first already fixed. |
| M4-D44 | `doctor fix --dry-run` returns a token that a later `doctor fix --if-match` in another process can match: nothing run-specific (run id, tx id, backup path, ages) enters it. |
| M4-D54 | `actions.jsonl` is group-committed once per transaction, derived files are written without fsync, and directory fsyncs are deferred through owned handles to explicit barriers, each justified in writing because a crash matrix cannot test fsync placement. The journal stays write-ahead per step, as it is, and the target follows the counted boundaries. |
| M4-D56 | A semantic manifest of inputs and outputs is the frozen contract, compared with a released baseline that the documented updater never touches; member order is not contract. |
| M4-D57 | The first tag is `v0.1.0`, made by the checkpoint leaf after every criterion passes. The first released baseline is written, and the golden's header flips to `frozen: true`, in the same commit. |

### Defaults for questions the plan does not answer

When a bead meets a question its text does not settle, it applies these defaults in order, records the choice in a `decided: … because …` comment on the bead, and extends README if the choice changes a promise:

1. Prefer an existing error code, warning code, action or key to a new one.
2. Additive JSON, token-frugal by default. Detail goes behind `-v`.
3. Stable order: sorted by target id, then name, then path.
4. No network on a read path, except for commands whose job is upstream (`outdated`, `search`, `info`, `doctor --online`).
5. Every write through fsx, and every mutation through a transaction or a recorded settings line.
6. Fail closed on anything persisted that cannot be fully read.
7. Never ask the owner. Decide, write `decided: … because …`, and move on (CLAUDE.md "Blocked on a Human").

Choices a bead's author made while writing it are marked "Decided while writing this bead" in that bead; the implementer confirms or adjusts each in the close comment.

### How the plan was reviewed, and what filing added

- **The first review round.** Two independent reviews read the first draft in full: one checked every claim about the code against `c0ab5e9`, and the other checked internal consistency and the vision's coverage. Among their findings were three designs that would not have worked as first written: Tukui plans that could never be applied, bound runs that skipped the token check on their no-op paths and in dry runs, and a plan lock the existing lock code cannot build.
- **The second review round** (seventeen revisions and four delivery corrections) read the plan as it stood after the first review (the decision log calls it "the reviewed draft") and asked of each protocol whether it guarantees what it claims. It found that the commit lock still compared only generations, that two applications of one plan could split it, that a two-rename flatten was journaled as one step, that a set-aside journal could be restored over newer work, that gc deleted by age alone, that the deferred directory syncs depended on paths a rename can invalidate, that the golden's own update mode could erase the evidence of a breaking change, that the guide's stamp had no fixed point and broke the skill's frontmatter, and that `remove dbm retail` could remove DBM from another client before explaining the mistake. Each is now a decision and an owned leaf. The facts both rounds established, each confirmed in the source, are in the ground-truth comment; what they changed in the graph is in the delivery comment.
- **What filing added.** Area T and its four leaves, at the owner's request for comprehensive unit tests and end-to-end test scripts with detailed logging (the test and logging standard above); the subtasks of most leaves; the edges from T1 to every bead that writes integration tests; and the recomputed graph above. The planning and filing record is the last of the plan's comments on this epic.
